p: I, I think we're quite honestly, the law passed 6 years ago. So we've just been hustling to get to 2025 and 2030.
Right.
Uh, now that we are kind of getting to that point where we can safely say we're pretty confident we're gonna hit 50% by '30, now we're planning for the future, so.

Um, on solar, you've established a goal of 100 megawatts of solar, uh, on

city-owned buildings by 2030 and 150 megawatts by the end of 2035. That's the 90 local law 99.
Yep.

How much has been installed? How much is set to be installed? And what funding do you have? And I guess one of my questions would be, again, you have your DCAS buildings, but do you also help the other buildings of which there are many?
Yes uh, especially schools. Uh, so to date—
Oh, I was gonna ask about schools, yeah.

The city has completed over 204 solar installations, which is about 33.5 megawatts. 50% of the capacity is in disadvantaged communities. And we have in our pipeline 39.5 megawatts, um, across 134 projects, 63% of which are, um, in disadvantaged communities. And we're working very hard to identify other sites. Um, uh, these are basically sites that don't require roof repair— repairs generally. Um, is, is the ideal. Um, so, um, we, we do believe that we are on track, uh, and have the funding to do 100 by 2030.

Okay. I mean, this is a silly question, but again, the federal government, I don't think he likes wind. He doesn't like air. He doesn't like sunshine. So is it hard to get solar equipment? Obviously, I hear about the EV, but I didn't know if it's hard to— I don't know.

Yeah I mean, I think one of the things that, um, uh, has sort of, you know, has the potential to impact is the, um, there was a, a federal credit for solar, um, that has gone away. Um, but, uh, I don't know if you want to add anything about the supply chain.
No, I think, um, this again, going back to '90s— '97 passing in 2019, shortly after that was COVID, shortly after that is supply and supply chain disruptions.
Right?

Basically this entire time since then. So, uh, yes, it, it can be an issue and can be a cause. We haven't seen it be major at this point though, so far. 'Cause you are the ones who'll be buying quite a bit of solar equipment, I would imagine.

Um, we are proud of the progress we've made so far, uh, in spite of these challenges. So I, I don't think we're at the, at the point where we would say it's stopped us or blocked us, but it's something to navigate as we're continuing forward, yeah.

Okay. That's helpful. Um, in terms of lighting, the Preliminary Commitment Plan includes $630.9 million uh, for 5 years, over 5 years for direct installation of lighting systems in the schools. So how many schools does this funding provide for? Um, can you provide a list? Not necessarily right now. What's the scope of this program? What's the completion of this program? And I, I believe there's another $300 million planned for other DOE lighting projects. Can you provide a list and a timeline for the projects funded? And you just basically— how many schools and how much it costs?
So I think you're talking about the direct install program.
Yeah.

So we've completed lighting upgrades in 367 schools and we have 433 to go, um, to achieve the 800-school target. Um, and, uh, we've

allocated $630 million in the Capital Plan to complete up to 800 additional schools after the original target is met. Do you want anything?
Okay, so you feel that you're on schedule, basically.
Yes, as with all things, we are, uh, working as fast as possible.
Okay. The Citywide Resiliency Measures East Side Coastal Resilient Project, a project that you and I know very, very well.
I do indeed.

I feel like I have gray hair from that project. Um, so the, uh, Preliminary Plan, the PCCB, includes $432.5 million across 5 years for citywide resiliency measures as part of this plan. What is the scope of the project, and what's the estimated timetable and completion? Now, you just have a small portion of it. It's a much bigger plan. Mhm. But how are you involved and what's going on from your perspective?
Yeah. Um, I will, I will just say this is a, actually, a DDC-managed project. So, um, I'll have to defer to them on some of the details here.
Okay, alright. 70 Mulberry, another project that you and I know very well.
Yes.

Because we spent some time when the fire took place, horrible fire. So it was $149.1 million across 5 years for reconstruction of 70 Mulberry. Can you give us an update? Can you tell us about the scope? Um, what's gonna happen in the future? Um, I know it's not happening as fast as people would like, put it that way.
Yeah and, um, again, I'm not trying to pass the buck, but this is also a DDC-managed project.
So you don't have anything to do with either one of these?
Um, I mean, ultimately we will, but, uh, in terms of the actual construction, yeah.
Managing 70 Mulberry for sure.
Yeah, yeah, they're, they're currently in the process of amending the CP um, and they're working with OMB on that, um, $21 million. So the budget passes through our budget.
Correct.
So $21 million has been registered already. Um, I believe they're waiting on that amended CP to, um, continue. But we would get more specific timelines from DDC on that.
Okay, yeah, you can ask them to, um, Staten Island. I know it is Frank's— yeah, he's gonna ask. Go, Frank, you ask the Staten Island question. Not the forgotten borough though. Go ahead.

Well, for starters, uh, since I have the opportunity, I'd love to ask about the, uh, the status of the borough flag that used to be atop of, uh, City Hall and, uh, I know that was discontinued and wondering if there was a financial reason for that, or what our chances of getting each borough's flag flying above City Hall again might be.
Yeah, so, um, I did look into this and actually that falls under City Hall operations of the building, so it's not, um, a DCAS, uh, decision.

Fair enough. Um, so in terms of, uh, Staten Island, the Preliminary Capital Commitment Plan includes $202 million, uh, across the 5-year plan, uh, for Staten Island's master plan, uh, the Phase 2 renovations. Uh, what's the scope of the work being done?
Which— sorry, which building are we talking about?
This is, uh, this is a Court Capital project.
Okay. Project.
Um, also, this is one of the ones where it's in our budget, but we're not actively managing it. Um, it's being managed with OMB and state
Understood.
Yep.
Got it. Let me see what else am I— give me a moment, Chair, to— thank you.

I can ask— please. Uh, just, um, I'm very excited about your tours I have to say. So you have money for 1 position increasing to $172,000 for 2 positions to go to the top of 1 Center Street. So what are the 2 positions? What are they going to be doing? Um, and then, uh, just talk a little bit about the $6 million, which is the capital amount to do— I guess you're going to put fences. We didn't believe in fences. We just did it. So I'm glad you have a little fence around it. Go ahead.

Yeah. So there are, I guess, 2 pieces to this. So the first is the personnel. Um, we have, as you noted, we have 2 people that we're hiring for this. One is, um, for IT to support the actual sort of reservation system. Um, we need somebody to actually maintain that system. Um, and then the other is, um, a DCAS police officer who will help escort the tours up. Um, and so, um, that's what the two positions are. Um, in terms of the $6 million, um, you know, one of the things we're, we're touting, of course, the public access that will be— the people will be able to reserve from the City Store but, um, the City Store and online, actually. Say, um, but, um, the $6 million obviously encompasses a much broader set of work including, um, redoing the facade and sort of repairing the, um, the, the tiles up there and stuff like that. So, um, it's really, um, you know, a broader project that is about sort of restoring the cupola in general for future generations and making sure that it's able to sort of have a longer lifespan. So we're excited to do that work.
That elevator is pretty small.
It is a small elevator, yes.
Spin on it.
Yes, intimate. I think that's what we like to say.
Very. Yes, you're gonna— you'll have enough reservations-wise, I guess, your limit to be able to access the elevator.
It's, it's, it's 5 per tour, and then plus the, um, person who will be accompanying them.
Okay.
I have one more, Chair. Yeah, if you would.
Go ahead.

Thank you. Uh, as obviously you know, DCAS manages the city's real estate portfolio and helps determine where agencies locate offices and services. Staten Island residents, uh, as the Chair was kind enough to point out, we often feel like our borough is forgotten.
Yes.

And that, uh, we get fewer government service locations than other parts of the city. How does DCAS consider borough equity when

deciding where to place new agency offices or leased facilities? And are there opportunities to expand city services on Staten Island?

Yeah, absolutely. I mean, um, you know, as we are sort of approaching every lease, we're obviously thinking about two things. One is, um, how do we get the best deal for our taxpayers, and also about the operations of city agencies and what works for, you know, whatever service they're providing. Um, but I'll, um, turn it to my Executive Deputy Commissioner to sort of add some detail there.

So in general, we - we work with the agencies to determine what their catchment area is, and they use their, um, you know, whatever their needs are in either the public-facing services might dictate where they need to be or their core operations or headquarters need to be. So certainly, I-I, if there's something that you think, um, an agency needs to, you know, have a, an additional presence, then we can talk about that and work with the agency to see what that would look like.

Just, uh, sitting here the other day at the Department for the Aging, there was a discussion about 14 Wall Street, hmm, and the fact that it seemed really expensive in terms of their moving from as an agency into there. I think that somebody from the public or from a Council Member asked that it was almost as expensive as the entire budget of the agency. So can you talk a little bit about 14 Wall Street, how that got determined as a location, and, you know, how you're gonna look at it in the future? Because I'm sure it's lovely for the Department for the Aging, but we're all trying to figure out how to save money. So, yeah, I think— the best deal we could get?

I'm not, um, you know, we, we did see, um, our sister agency testify, and I think we weren't sure, um, what number that was referring to. But I will say that the way that we do, um, leasing, we think of it in terms of the, like, term of the lease, um, usually when it's a budget number. So it may seem larger than it actually is. It's not an annualized number. So that was my guess that

that's maybe what the reaction is to that, um, the specifics of that deal. I will just say, you know, um, I know, uh, er, one of the first things that I did when I started was I, um, went over to 2 Lafayette just to see the DYFTA space and sort of assess the conditions there. And I know that they're very anxious to get into newly renovated space. So, um, that obviously is something that we're, we're, um, very anxious to do for them.

Okay. Um, and then I know we heard earlier about the need to, uh, do applications and information about civil service. There were, uh, er, ah, hmm, there was a story in the city the other day about 31 people hired from the 80,000 people who applied for the Mandami Administration. This was pre— —coming into office. I know that. So my question is, I don't know if it's possible to have some conversation with those 80,000 applicants. 31 were hired from that list. So to say, sorry, you can apply for civil service, that wouldn't make sense because you need— er, or maybe they're not interested. Who knows? Is

there some way to do that or is that not possible? Software-wise or some other way?

Yeah, we're, um, looking into that. That was actually a question that I asked when I, um, started as well. Um, uh, you know, I think it's a separate system obviously from, from the hiring that we do, but, um, obviously if there's an opportunity to sort of do something there, we'd, we'd be very open to it. Um, it's just, you know, I think a question of, um, you know, where that data is stored and, and how easy it is to sort of speak to, um, between the two systems.

Alright, I think that's helpful. I think the main takeaway for me is you need more money to buy more electric vehicles and so I would say that that is the takeaway that we— that I have from this conversation. Thank you very much. And, uh, we look forward to the next, uh, the law department.
Yes, thank you.

Alright, thank you very much for being here, Law Department. So this, uh, hearing will be with the Law Department. We had DCAS before, as you know. I wanna welcome the newly confirmed but

not new Corporation Counsel, Steve Banks. The Law Department's Fiscal '27 Preliminary Budget is $345.1 million. It's my understanding, which is $68.3 million more than the Fiscal '26 Adopted Budget, and it's partly due to funding in the Preliminary Plan for additional attorneys and support staff, which are desperately needed. The Law Department, as we know, represents the city, the Mayor, city agencies, City Council, and other city elected officials in civil litigation matters. The Preliminary Plan includes $46.1 million in new needs, growing to $67.2 million in FY27 and in the out years for additional legal staff at the agency, court-appointed monitors, which are also expensive, and special masters, which are expensive, and for the remediation manager costs mandated for the Department of Correction. I look forward to learning more today. We all know how the Law Department plans to hire for the new positions, how they will be used to save the city money on tort liability in particular, and how the agency will respond to the Mayor's savings mandate. And I'm delighted that Council Member Stevens is here.

So now you need— who's on? Ah, yeah, Santosuosso is on. She is having a baby soon, and so she's not here. We're very excited about the baby.
Not right now.
No, but soon.
Yeah, hmm, she looks like she is right now.
Soon. Uh, you need to be sworn in. Go ahead.

Alright, we will now hear testimony from the Administration. Before we begin, I will administer the oath of affirmation. Panelists, please raise your right hand. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this Committee, and to respond honestly to Council Member questions?
Yes.
Alright, you may begin when ready.

Thank you. Good afternoon, uh, Chair Brewer, members of the Committee, uh, as well as other members of the Council who may come during the course of the hearing. It's a pleasure to come before you to discuss the Law Department's Fiscal

Year 2027 Preliminary Budget. I'm joined by First Assistant Corporation Counsel Sheryl Neufeld, uh, Managing Attorney Eric Eichenholz, and Chief Administration, uh, Chief of Administration Jenny Nagle-Yndigoyen. Uh, the Law Department represents the city, the Mayor, the City Council, other elected officials, and the city's agencies in all affirmative and defensive civil litigation. The department brings proceedings in family court, uh, uh, with alleging violations of criminal laws and represents the people of the state of New York in proceedings filed in the criminal court to enforce the City's Administrative Code. Law Department attorneys draft and review local and state legislation, real estate leases, procurement contracts, financial instruments for the sale of municipal bonds. The department also provides legal counsel to city officials on a wide range of issues such as civil rights, education, intellectual property, land use, and environmental prop— uh, policy. The department's work embraces all entities and operations. Our work impacts all areas of daily living in New York City.

The department currently has approximately 785 assistant corporation counsels and 600 legal support professionals. We're proud to be a leader in the legal profession with approximately 31% of our lawyers racially and ethnically diverse and 58% women. Over the past few years, headcount reductions have impaired the Law Department's ability to fulfill its mission in representing the city, its elected officials, including the Council, and other city entities. The 200 new attorney lines and 100 professional support lines provided to the Law Department in the proposed budget will be allocated to support all areas of the Law Department. This increased staffing will help mitigate the increases in monetary settlements and payouts resulting from a number of factors, including the Law Department's reduced headcount in the past Administration. The increase in staff will allow us to restore our ability to settle meritorious cases earlier and make dispositive motions and try cases that lack merit, reducing payouts in both types of cases. Other new staff will focus on enhancing the Law

Department's ability to advise and support the city through legal advice, uh, and affirmative litigation initiatives. This new staffing will also enable the department to increase the provision of risk assessments in order to help agencies reform practices and avert litigation against the city in the first place. Through all of this, we'll advance the city's affordability agenda as well as the interests of the city, the Mayor, the Council, and other elected officials. A large focus of the Law Department's work this past year has been addressing potential challenges regarding federal funding requirements which have changed and evolved rapidly over the past year. To do so, we have set up a special team to focus exclusively on these emerging, emerging challenges. Our work has already been critical safeguarding billions of dollars in federal grants that touch on all aspects of municipal life, including infrastructure, policing, housing, social services, and mission-critical objectives such as disaster mitigation and counterterrorism efforts.

With the increased staffing, we'll be positioned to litigate affirmatively and defensively to protect the city's rights and interests. For example, we brought a lawsuit to protect funding the city received from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, FEMA, in accordance with federal law to reimburse the city for services to asylum seekers. We sued to protect New York City Public Schools magnet school funding that was cut based upon reported violations of Title IX due to the public school's guidelines to support transgender and gender-expansive students. We also joined coalitions of other cities and states to challenge grant conditions that violated federal law because they intended to commandeer, uh, the recipients to enforce federal immigration policy and federal executive orders, among other things. Similarly, we filed and joined more than 25 amicus briefs on topics such as immigration enforcement, federal funding, deployment of the National Guard, and New Yorkers' rights and benefits to ensure that the city's voice is heard as courts consider these emergent legal issues, even in circumstances in which the city is not a party.

At my confirmation hearing before the Council last month, I emphasized the importance of the Law Department being promptly attentive to the needs of all of its individual and institutional clients, including the Council and Council Members. Since assuming the position of Corporation Counsel, I'm pleased to report that we have been working in collaboration with the Speaker and the Council in a number of areas. Individual members of the Council have also reached out to me directly to discuss matters of concern. Our office will continue to work side by side with Council staff on crafting legislation, providing legal advice in a timely manner, and ensuring legal clarity and defensibility in doing so. An excellent example of this is our recent work together on procurement reform legislation. The Department's work in both revenue saving— is both revenue saving and revenue generating. For example, in FY25, the Department saved the city $128 million by resolving $140 million in claims and contractual disputes for a total payment of only $12 million.

Similarly, the Department's defense of real property tax assessments protected $96 million in property tax receipts in FY25 and almost $65 million during the first half of FY26, which prever— preserve funding for city services. During this Fiscal year so far, the Department has recovered over $35 million for the city in and his entities. This includes monetary recoveries for property damage, breach of contract, restitution, False Claims Act cases, securities fraud, public health and safety matters, including anti-youth vaping, uh, and tenant protection code enforcement cases, and opioid settlement payments, among other things. In this Fiscal Year, collection law firms supervised by the Division have, uh, recovered another— $30 million. In addition to recovering monetary damages, the Department sues to enjoin unlawful and harmful practices that cause or contributed to a public nuisance or otherwise negatively affect public health and safety. For example, we are currently litigating against Kia and Hyundai over their failure to install industry-standard engine immobilizing technology in

low-end models of their vehicles, which, when highlighted as part of a TikTok challenge led to massive spikes in thefts of those models in the city, as well as dangerous driving, property damage, injuries, and deaths. We're also currently litigating against 4 major social media companies for harms that have resulted in the mental health of young people and the cost of those harms imposed on the city as a result of the deliberate design, marketing, and operation of addicted social media platforms, which intend to nationally target youth. And as reported yesterday, we recently obtained a ruling assessing $2.1 million in fines against a landlord who has failed to make repairs to a residential building and $1,000 in ongoing daily fines until the conditions are corrected. These cases and other litigation aim to change behavior by compelling compliance with city law and policy to enhance public health and safety and to protect New Yorkers from unlawful and harmful conduct. We also anticipate saving the city over $1 million in this Fiscal Year in payments from the Judgment and Claims Fund through our continuing

activity to compel insurance companies to defend and identify the city. This program, which began in the late 1990s, has saved more than $3 billion in judgments and claims payments through insurance takeovers since its inception. Every case that the insurance company steps in to defend is a case that does not have to be defended by city attorneys, thus saving enormous legal resources. Settlements and judgments paid by insurers in cases falling within policy coverage also save the city substantial sums. The Law Department also represents the city in more than 70,000 cases annually. We continue to experience an increase in pending cases. Approximately half of our pending cases, some 35,000 involve tort matters. These pending cases include a large number of Adult Survivor Act and Child Victims Act cases, and we anticipate a continued influx of these cases which involve claims of misconduct that occurred many years ago. We also expect a continued increase in Gender Motivated Violence Act cases with claims for past conduct. Given the significant impact of these cases on the city, we are looking for solutions to give the

city certainty regarding exposure while properly compensating survivors with meritorious claims. The Department also serves as the statutory mandated presentment agency for all juvenile justice, adolescent offender, interstate child support cases referred to the New York City Family Court. Under the Rehabilitative Mandate of the Family Court Act, the Department must work to achieve outcomes that serve the needs of each individual young person brought before the court, while at the same time protecting the interests of crime victims and ensuring the safety of the community at large. Law Department attorneys also appear in the New York City Family Courts to handle petitions to establish parentage and obtain, modify, or enforce existing child support orders. Uh, in 2025, Justice, uh, juvenile justice case referrals increased by 11%, um, from, uh, 77, uh, ah, hmm, 7,740 to 6,964 referrals, uh, in 2024. 66% of the referrals represent felony charges. In 2025, there were 348 firearms cases referred to the Department, which is a decrease of 15% from 411 firearms cases in 2024. The number of child support referrals in 2025 remain virtually the same,

uh, with, uh, 1,889 child support referrals in 2024 and 1,894 in 2025. My testimony today provides an overview of the very broad and varied legal work performed by the Law Department. By keeping the interests of all New Yorkers at the center of our work, we can do what is right and just, solve problems, reinforce trust in government and help meet the needs of New Yorkers. I thank you for your support for the Law Department and look forward to our continued collaboration. Happy to answer any questions that you may have.
Thank you. We've been joined by the Speaker, and she has her first, uh, question, and then I'm gonna, uh, ask the woman, uh, who's having the baby soon for a question.

Ah, okay. Thank you, Chair. Um, so thank you, Steve, for being here. We appreciate it. Uh, got a couple questions for you. The 9/11 files, as you know, this is something that is very important to the City Council. The fact that the city has sat on these 9/11 files for years, the fact that thousands of people, uh, became sick and died of cancer because the city did not, um, disclose

the fact that the air was not safe to breathe, um, in conjunction with the federal EPA and former EPA head Christy Todd Whitman. So my question is, and I had asked this during the confirmation hearing, what is the status of the release of the 9/11 files?

Uh, thank you for that question. I can report that since I was, uh, confirmed a couple of weeks ago, we have set up a team that is reviewing what documents can be posted on a portal to provide access to the public and the cost for maintaining such public access, uh, and what documents cannot be posted. For example, documents with, uh, personal information or individual— of individuals such as medical information. We're also looking at the cost of determining what documents can and cannot be posted. We will keep you posted on what we are doing, but that's what we've done the last several weeks, and we're working on this very hard to be able to, as I said, post documents available to the public, having made a determination of which ones, uh, can't be posted and which ones can, with the ones that can't be really ones that involve individual, uh, people's, uh,

personal identifying information in their medical records.

I mean, obviously we don't wanna post people's personal identifying information, but I'm gonna urge you and the law department to be as fulsome as possible in the release of the records. How quickly will that portal be up and running, and how quickly do you think that the documents will be released to the public?

I think the key fact here, uh, you have my commitment to be as fulsome as possible, but I think the key factor is there are tens of thousands of documents and to review them properly so we don't have a repeat of what just happened when the federal government released records. We wanna make sure that what we release are in fact not, uh, revealing people's personal information.

Okay. I'm gonna ask that you update my office directly with this so that we understand when the portal is up and running, which documents have been released so that we are aware of the timeline and that when these documents are actually public.
Uh, absolutely. We'll keep you advised.

Thank you. I know, I appreciate that. Um, the second question I have followed up on something I asked you in the confirmation hearing, which is on Timothy Pearson, and is the law department still representing Mr. Pearson?

I have reviewed Timothy Pearson's right to legal representation at the city's expense under the general municipal law and for related matters. Based upon my review of new evidence since the original decisions were made, I have determined that he is not entitled to representation by the city in these matters. Thus, the city will no longer pay for Mr. Pearson's legal representation. Similarly, based on my review of new evidence, I have also determined that Jeffrey Madry is not entitled to representation under the general municipal law in the 4 lawsuits involving allegations against Mr. Pearson. As such, the city will no longer pay for Mr. Madry's legal representation in those matters.

This is excellent. I wanna commend you. I wanna commend, uh, the law department for reaching what is the right decision in this matter. Neither Mr. Pearson nor Mr. Madry should have ever been represented by the city law department. And I hope that then this will serve as a clear warning sign that, that those types of representations, which are clearly compromised, will not happen again. So thank you for doing that.
I appreciate it. Thank you for, uh, asking me to do it, and thank you for the right—

I have one last question, which is, um, having worked at the City Law Department, which is something I'm incredibly proud of that experience, I know the importance of all the work that you're doing and you're serving also as our counsel, which we really appreciate, the agency counsel, all the work that the Law Department does in so many different areas. You have a lot of vacancies. What's the status of the filling of those vacancies? What are the plans to do so?

Uh, thank you for that question as well. So, uh, we are very pleased to have, uh, 200 attorney lines and, uh, 100, uh, support professional

lines in the budget. Uh, we, uh, I have experience, by the way, with hiring 200 lawyers when I was at the Legal Aid Society for a very relatively short period of time. We have an excellent in-house recruitment team that is already well advanced in terms of recruiting the class of entry-level, uh, assistant, uh, corporation counsels. And we are on track for the things we've been doing internally, uh, to hire significant numbers of staff over the course of the next number of months. Uh, we will complete this, uh, certainly during this fiscal year or this coming fiscal year, FY27, and as soon as possible during the fiscal year because of the urgent need to fill, uh, these positions in order to do, uh, two things. One is to fill lines that have been hollowed out, uh, as a result of the last administration. Uh, the need for those kinds of, uh, uh, lawyers is prevalent in when we look at things like judgment and claims, uh, but also we wanna make sure that we have, uh, enough lawyers to take on the kinds of things that we think, uh, will help New Yorkers in their everyday lives.

Like, for example, the announcement yesterday of the $2.1 million, uh, fines and $1,000 a day fines, uh, with respect to a landlord on the worst landlords list. So we have two goals. One is to be able to, uh, return ourselves to the strength that we think is needed, and two, to be able to be, uh, ready to move forward with the kinds of needs that New Yorkers have. And appreciate your championing, uh, the Law Department, given your, your role as a Speaker, but also your role as a former member of the Law Department.
Great, thank you so much. Those are my questions. Thank you.

I just want to follow up on 9/11. So, um, it's— I really do appreciate the fact that you understand the importance of this. It was, uh, certainly the, uh, DOI that I think got the discussion started before you started. And, uh, when I was Chair of Oversight and Investigations, and now I understand that there's, uh, there was an answer to a FOIL. Now there's a response. So that's sort of what you're going on in terms of the timeframe, trying to figure out the previous response that the

law department made on FOIL and now you're taking up when they've, um, sent a second letter.

Yeah, I think there's a, a— and I appreciate that you had reached out to me, would have conversations about this. I think that the challenge is to address the situation which is built up over several, several decades. Uh, we want to be expeditious, we want to be fast, we want to be responsible. Uh, the FOIL law, uh, has much tighter time frames than, uh, we can, uh, be responsible in responding to. So we wanna be respectful of the people that file the recent FOIL requests, respond to them, and try to address their concerns in the context of whatever appeal they're filing. But you have on the record what we're attempting to do. Uh, might there be disputes about, uh, how fast we're acting? Uh, I think the Speaker has made it clear that, uh, and we do speak quite frequently, that this will be a topic of our, uh, ongoing conversations, and maybe that will give some, uh, solace to the people who are pressing for these documents. As I said at my confirmation hearing, this is also personal to me. My daughter, uh, then in the 5th

grade, was at school on Chambers and Greenwich Street, was one of the young children evacuated as the buildings were coming down. So, uh, I am well aware of how urgent it is that we should act, and we are moving with, with urgency.
Thank you and that's great news about Mr. Pearson, Mr. Andre, um, do you know how much money we would be saving or how much money has already been allocated to their, uh, legal assistance?
The total amount that had already been, uh, paid out in these cases that I was referring to was approximately $645,000.
Okay, so that'll be— that's what will be saved in the future plus. Okay.
Um, just for the record, uh, uh, Chair, just we can't predict exactly how much it would have been. It could be spending it at a higher rate, spending at a lower rate.
We don't know.
